summary: This standards-track document defines how Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) markings used on wired IP networks are mapped to the User Priority values of IEEE 802.11 wireless networks. Without an agreed mapping, quality-of-service markings can be lost or misapplied when traffic crosses between wired and Wi-Fi segments. It gives implementers a consistent set of mappings so priority treatment carries over.

plainLanguage.summary: IP networks and Wi-Fi use different markings to give traffic priority. This RFC explains how to translate those markings so traffic receives a suitable queue on both networks.

what access category does ef map to in wifi
why is default dscp to up mapping wrong
should an access point trust client dscp markings
subtitle: Recommended translations that preserve traffic priorities as IP packets cross into Wi-Fi.

tldr.problem: IP networks mark traffic with six-bit DSCP values, while Wi-Fi uses three-bit User Priorities. Common shortcuts map several important traffic classes to the wrong Wi-Fi queue.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends explicit downstream mappings from Diffserv service classes to Wi-Fi User Priorities. For upstream traffic, it prefers that the access point apply its own administrative DSCP policy.
tldr.outcome: The mappings are recommendations that administrators may override. RFC 8325 has been updated by RFC 8622 and RFC 9956.

today: RFC 8325 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2018. It has been updated by RFC 8622 and RFC 9956; consult those RFCs for later changes.

sections.title: Why Wired and Wi-Fi Priorities Differ
sections.content:
Wired IP networks use a Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) to mark each packet's service class. IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi uses a three-bit User Priority (UP). The RFC defines recommended translations so the intended treatment can continue across the wireless access point.

Wi-Fi uses four access categories, and its shared radio channel cannot guarantee the same service as the Expedited Forwarding or Assured Forwarding behaviors used by Diffserv. The access point may be at the edge of the Diffserv network or may connect other network infrastructure over Wi-Fi, so the appropriate mapping depends on its role.

The RFC focuses on Wi-Fi infrastructure, including autonomous access points, controller-managed systems, wireless backhaul and mesh networks. It treats the separate mapping plan in RFC 7561 as a different Diffserv domain that needs translation at the boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: IP and Wi-Fi use different markings for traffic priority. The access point must translate between them, and Wi-Fi cannot promise every service that a wired network can provide.

sections.title: Why the Default Translation Loses Meaning
sections.content:
A common shortcut copies the three most significant bits of a DSCP value into the three UP bits. This puts Expedited Forwarding voice traffic in the Video category, and can place streaming video and broadcast video in Best Effort. It also sends Operations, Administration, and Maintenance traffic to Background.

The common reverse shortcut multiplies UP by eight to construct a DSCP. Since it maps three bits to six, it cannot preserve all of the distinctions among Diffserv classes. For example, it merges conferencing and real-time interactive traffic into the same DSCP.

The RFC therefore recommends an explicit mapping based on the Diffserv service classes. This better preserves the intended categories, though Wi-Fi's contention process remains random and cannot guarantee the behavior of wired per-hop services.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual shortcuts can put traffic in the wrong queue and erase distinctions between service classes. An explicit mapping preserves more of the intended meaning.

sections.title: Recommended Downstream Mappings
sections.content:
For traffic moving from wired IP to Wi-Fi, the RFC recommends mapping Telephony marked EF and VOICE-ADMIT to UP 6. Signaling marked CS5 maps to UP 5. Conferencing, real-time interactive, streaming and broadcast video map to UP 4.

Low-Latency Data marked AF2x maps to UP 3. OAM marked CS2, High-Throughput Data marked AF1x and Standard traffic marked DF map to UP 0. Low-Priority Data marked CS1 maps to UP 1. Network Control marked CS6 and CS7 maps to UP 7 when the access point serves network infrastructure; security guidance recommends UP 0 when Wi-Fi is the network edge. Unused codepoints should map to UP 0.

The IEEE mapping from UP to access category is fixed: UP 6 and 7 use Voice, 4 and 5 use Video, 0 and 3 use Best Effort, and 1 and 2 use Background. Administrators may change the recommended DSCP-to-UP mappings to suit their network.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice uses UP 6, video uses UP 4, and ordinary traffic uses UP 0. Network control traffic needs different handling depending on whether the access point connects network infrastructure or only client devices.

sections.title: Upstream Mapping and Marking
sections.content:
For traffic moving from Wi-Fi to the wired network, client software can map DSCP to UP, or an access point can map UP to DSCP or pass through the packet's DSCP. The RFC says an access point MUST NOT derive upstream DSCP from a UP value chosen by a wireless client.

When policy allows client markings to pass through, the RFC recommends preserving the Layer 3 DSCP rather than rebuilding it from the less detailed UP. It generally does not recommend accepting DSCP markings from unauthenticated or unauthorized devices. CS6 and CS7 should not pass upstream unless an administrator specifically permits them.

The preferred option is for the access point to act as the Diffserv boundary and set or reset DSCP according to administrative policy. A QoS Map element can also tell clients the DSCP-to-UP mapping; the recommended baseline maps each UP to DSCP zero, with exceptions for codepoints in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The access point should enforce the network's own policy for traffic leaving Wi-Fi. It should not trust priority markings from unauthorized clients.

sections.title: Protecting Priority Queues
sections.content:
A device or application can mark traffic to request higher priority, intentionally or by mistake. The RFC recommends conditioning traffic from unauthorized sources and changing unapproved markings to Default Forwarding or UP 0. It also recommends policing EF traffic flows.

Wi-Fi clients share the radio channel with the access point. A client that can mark traffic to UP 4 through UP 7 could take a disproportionate share of airtime. Network operators should control which devices and traffic classes can use those priorities, and map unauthorized codepoints to UP 0.

In a Wi-Fi-at-the-edge deployment, CS6 and CS7 are not normally needed by client devices. Mapping them to UP 0 helps protect both Wi-Fi service and network-control traffic. Authentication, access control and rate limiting can provide additional protection.
sections.plainLanguage: High priority markings can let one device crowd out other traffic. The network should limit who can use them and lower markings that its policy does not authorize.
